segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “And to the angel of the assembly in Sardis write: These are the words of the one who has the seven spirits of God and the seven stars: I know your works—you have a name for being alive, yet you are dead.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Wake up, and strengthen what remains, which was about to die, for I have not found your works complete before my God.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Remember, then, how you received and heard; keep it, and turn back. If you do not wake up, I will come like a thief, and you will never know at what hour I will come upon you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But you have a few names in Sardis who have not soiled their garments, and they will walk with me in white, for they are worthy.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The one who conquers will be clothed like this in white garments, and I will never erase their name from the book of life, and I will acknowledge their name before my Father and before his angels.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit is saying to the assemblies.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “And to the angel of the assembly in Philadelphia write: These are the words of the Holy One, the True One, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I know your works—look, I have set before you an open door that no one is able to shut—that you have little power, and yet you kept my word and did not deny my name.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Look, I am giving some from the synagogue of Satan—those who say they are Jews and are not, but are lying—look, I will make them come and bow down before your feet, and they will know that I have loved you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Because you kept my word about endurance, I also will keep you from the hour of testing that is about to come upon the whole world, to test those who live on the earth.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I am coming soon. Hold on to what you have, so that no one takes your crown.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I will make the one who conquers a pillar in the sanctuary of my God, and they will never again go outside; and I will write on them the name of my God and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which comes down out of heaven from my God, and my own new name.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit is saying to the assemblies.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “And to the angel of the assembly in Laodicea write: These are the words of the Amen, the faithful and true witness, the beginning of God’s creation:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot. I wish you were cold or hot!

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So, because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I am about to vomit you out of my mouth.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Because you say, ‘I am rich; I have grown rich and need nothing,’ and you do not know that you are the one who is wretched and pitiable and poor and blind and naked,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I advise you to buy from me gold refined by fire so that you may be rich, and white garments so that you may clothe yourself and the shame of your nakedness may not be exposed, and salve to rub on your eyes so that you may see.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: All those I love, I reprove and discipline. So be zealous and turn back.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Look, I am standing at the door and knocking. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to them and dine with them, and they with me.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: To the one who conquers I will grant to sit with me on my throne, just as I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit is saying to the assemblies.”

notes.note: The Greek word means “messenger” and is the ordinary word for an angel. Most scholars take it here as a heavenly being who represents the community, since the word means “angel” everywhere else in Revelation. Others take it as a human messenger or leader of the community. The letter addresses this figure in the singular “you” but plainly speaks to the whole community.

The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and, in the Greek Old Testament, for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and is well understood, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so that the reader sees one word for one Greek word.

Most translations keep “repent” as the established term. In modern English that word centers on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. “Turn back” is used for that reason.

“Names” here means persons, an idiom also found in Acts, and most modern versions translate “a few people.” The literal word is kept because the letter plays on it throughout: Sardis has a “name” for being alive (verse 1), a few “names” are unsoiled, and the conqueror’s “name” will not be erased but acknowledged (verse 5).

The verb is the ordinary Greek word for winning a battle, a contest or a lawsuit. The King James tradition has “overcometh,” and several modern versions keep “overcome,” while others use “conquer” in Revelation. The meaning is not disputed; “conquer” is chosen because it keeps the note of victory that “overcome” has largely lost.

The wording echoes Isaiah 22:22, where the steward Eliakim is given the key of the house of David, so that what he opens no one shuts and what he shuts no one opens. The image is of sole authority to admit to or exclude from the royal household, here applied to the risen Christ and the kingdom.

The Greek conjunction can mean “that” or “because.” The translation follows the punctuation of the Greek edition, which treats the open door as a parenthesis, so that the clause states what Christ knows. The other reading is “I have set before you an open door … because you have little power and yet have kept my word.”

The same phrase is used in the letter to Smyrna (2:9). It reflects a bitter local dispute between the Christ-believing assembly, many of whose members were themselves Jews, and the Jewish community in the city, over who truly belongs to God’s people. The language is polemic against particular opponents in a particular place, written by a Jewish author, and is not a statement about Jews as a people.

The verb names prostration in reverence, and what it signifies depends on who receives it. The King James Version has “worship before thy feet,” but the gesture here is made before human beings, so the physical act is translated, as in most modern versions. The scene reverses passages in Isaiah (such as 60:14) where the nations come and bow at Israel’s feet.

The Greek is literally “the word of my endurance.” It may mean Christ’s command to endure, which is the reading followed here and in many versions, or the message about Christ’s own endurance in suffering. The grammar allows both.

The same verb “keep” is used for the Philadelphians’ loyalty and Christ’s response. Whether “keep from the hour” means being spared the ordeal altogether or being protected through it is disputed; a similar phrase in John 17:15 is often cited for protection within the trial. The translation leaves the question open, as the Greek does.

Greek has two words that English Bibles usually both render “temple”: one for the whole complex with its courts, and this one for the building where God dwells. Most versions use “temple” here. “Sanctuary” is used throughout this translation to keep the two words distinct.

The Greek word can mean “beginning,” “origin” or “source,” or “ruler,” and translations are divided among them. “Beginning” is kept because Revelation uses the same word in the title “the beginning and the end” (21:6; 22:13). Many interpreters take the phrase to mean the one from whom creation originates, as in Colossians 1:15–18, and not the first thing created.

Both cold and hot are good here; the wish is that Laodicea were one or the other. Many scholars see an allusion to the local water supply: nearby Hierapolis had hot springs and Colossae cold fresh water, while Laodicea’s piped water arrived tepid. The older reading that “cold” means open hostility to Christ is now generally doubted.
The Greek verb means to vomit. Most English versions soften it to “spit” or the older “spew.” The stronger word is kept because the image is of drink so nauseating that the body rejects it.

The three things offered answer Laodicea’s own sources of pride. The city was a wealthy banking center, known for garments of glossy black wool, and the region was associated with a medical school and an eye remedy. Christ offers true wealth, white garments and sight to a community that thinks it lacks nothing.
